sentences.text: Mauriciosaurus was a small plesiosaur reaching approximately 2 meters in length, known from a single exceptionally well-preserved juvenile.
This short-necked reptile possessed a drop-shaped body and a small tail, making it look most like the polycotylids Trinacromerum and Dolichorhynchops.
Its upper jaws held at least 42 teeth on each side, with four located in the premaxilla and thirty-two in the maxilla.
Distinctive skeletal features include vertebrae with constricted outer surfaces and a coracoid bone lacking perforations along its midline and back margin.
Dark grey, rectangular structures found on the specimen likely represent scale-like tubercles that covered the underside of the animal.
The sole known specimen is owned by Mexican politician Mauricio Fernández Garza, though a replica is displayed at the Papalote Museo del Niño in Monterrey.
Remarkably, preserved soft tissue reveals a heavily pigmented lining protecting the internal organs from ultraviolet exposure.
Subcutaneous adipose tissue streamlined the body, while small neural spines suggest a tail cone of contour fat used for stabilization.
Workers at a quarry near Vallecillo in Nuevo León, Mexico, discovered the fossil material in the summer of 2011.
The genus was formally described in 2017 by Eberhard Frey, Eric Mulder, Wolfgang Stinnesbeck, Héctor Rivera Sylva, José Padilla Gutiérrez, and Arturo González González.
The description was based on a single well-preserved juvenile specimen approximately 2 meters long.
Dietary analysis suggests the animal hunted small prey, supported by its slender snout and small, pointed teeth.
Heavily muscled flippers with flexible skin edges likely acted as hydrofoils to enhance swimming efficiency.
Researchers estimate that Mauriciosaurus could swim at speeds similar to the modern leatherback sea turtle, reaching about 7 km/h.
In modern desert squamates, peritoneal pigmentation protects reproductive organs from solar radiation, a function hypothesized for this ancient marine reptile.
Thick contour fat in plesiosaurs like Mauriciosaurus may explain the rarity of preserved skin in the group.
Mauriciosaurus is classified as a genus of polycotylid plesiosaur within the family Polycotylidae.
Several unique features separate Mauriciosaurus from all other polycotylids, justifying its classification as a distinct genus.
The genus shares characteristics with Trinacromerum, Dolichorhynchops, and more basal polycotylids.
This extinct polycotylid plesiosaur lived in Mexico during the Late Cretaceous.
Biostratigraphic analysis dates the slab containing the fossil to the early Turonian portion of the Agua Nueva Formation.
Mauriciosaurus is the first known juvenile polycotylid preserved in an environment other than shallow water.

The animal fell into soft, water-soaked, anoxic sediment at temperatures between 21 and 37 degrees Celsius, conditions that preserved its skin. Anoxic conditions allowed subcutaneous fat to turn into adipocere, preserving the skin on the top half of Mauriciosaurus's body. Exposed parts of Mauriciosaurus's belly decayed before burial, causing the body cavity and gastralia to collapse.
